title: A mobile-first redesign for desktop-first teams
excerpt: Start a mobile first website redesign from the phone the founder actually checks. Decide what is cut, what stacks, and what stays easy to tap.
alt: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table. The phone is the width a desktop-first team has to design for first.
caption: The first screen is the one in the hand. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Does mobile-first mean desktop does not matter?
faqs.answer: The wide layout still gets a designed composition. It is the second frame, built from the same story with more room. Mobile-first means the phone is approved before that wide frame is polished, so the narrow screen is not a squeezed leftover.

faqs.question: What should be removed when a desktop page moves to a phone?
faqs.answer: Remove side columns, repeated explanations, and carousels that hide the offer behind a swipe. Keep the sentence that says what the company does, one primary action, and the proof that supports that action. Extra space on a large screen can show more of the same story.

faqs.question: How do we know the phone layout is good enough to ship?
faqs.answer: Read the first screen on the founder's actual phone, tap the action, and confirm the page does not jump when images load. The offer should be visible without pinching. If the only comfortable view is a scaled frame on a monitor, the pass is not done.

markdown:
A mobile first website redesign starts from the phone width the founder actually checks, then earns the wider layout. That phone is where a rushed visitor decides whether the offer is clear. A desktop composition that is squeezed down at the end keeps the decoration and loses the sentence.

Desktop-first teams are used to a wide frame. There is room for a side column, a large photograph, and a row of cards. That frame is a real screen, and it should still look considered. It is the second screen in the process. The first screen is the one in a pocket, glanced at between other things. Designing it first changes which words survive.

## Open the phone before the wide frame

Put the current site on the founder's phone. Note the width you are holding. Read the first screen without zooming. Write down what you can see: the words, the button, and whether your thumb can reach the control without shifting your grip.

Then sketch the new first screen at that width. One column. The offer in the first lines. One action. Proof, if it fits, as a short line. Everything else is a decision about order. Shrinking a wide poster until it fits is a different activity, and it produces a different page.

This is a method for the file, not a label on a desktop frame. If the design begins at a wide artboard and the phone frame is a derived copy, the team is still designing for the monitor. Flip the order. The phone frame is the one that must be approved before the wide frame is polished. Hanabi treats that narrow version as the composition the copy is written to fit.

## What gets cut

The phone has no side column. Navigation that was a horizontal list becomes a short menu, or a few links placed where they do not push the offer below the fold of a small screen. A hero that depended on a wide photograph has to work as a crop, or the photograph moves below the words so the offer is not trapped under an image.

Cut repeated explanations. If the headline says what the company does, the next block should add a fact, a proof, or a next step. Cut carousels that require a swipe before the offer is learnable. Cut footers that repeat the whole site map above the action a person came to take.

Cut motion that only plays well on a large screen. A sequence that pushes content around while someone is trying to read will feel worse in one hand. Keep the movement that shows a relationship, such as a panel opening, and keep it short. If the system asks for reduced motion, that movement should have a still alternative. The phone is where extra motion is most expensive.

Write the cuts down. The wide layout should not quietly restore every cut as a "desktop enhancement" that tells a different story. Extra room can hold a larger crop, a second column of the same proof, or more of the product in view. A different argument on a large screen is two sites sharing a domain.

## What stacks, and in which order

Stack in the order a person needs. The offer, then the action, then the proof that supports the action, then the detail. A desktop habit often places navigation, a large image, and a floating cluster of links in a composition that cannot be read from top to bottom. On a phone, top to bottom is the reading order you can count on. The first things in that order should be the things the brief named.

When a row of cards stacks, the first card is the one most people will see. Choose it on purpose. If the cards are truly equal, say so in the heading above them, and keep each card short enough that the second and third are a thumb-scroll away. A card that was a square on a wide screen often becomes a tall block. Check that the tall block still has one job.

Images need a stable box. A picture that loads and shoves the button down the page makes people miss the action, or tap the wrong thing while the page is still moving. Google's Core Web Vitals describe that movement as layout shift. The published targets are a CLS score under 0.1, largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, and interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds. [Google Search Central](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) is the reference for those thresholds. On a phone, a heavy hero and a button that jumps are the usual ways to miss them. Reserve the image's space. Keep the action in a place that does not move when the picture arrives.

## What must remain easy to tap

The primary action has to be a real control, with space around it so the neighboring link is hard to hit by mistake. Text links inside a paragraph can stay text. The thing you want someone to do should look like the thing to do, and it should sit where a thumb already is, or where the sentence has just made the case for it.

Forms go in one column. Labels sit with their fields, not inside the field as the only name. Error text appears next to the field that failed. A two-column form that looked efficient on a desktop becomes a puzzle on a phone when the labels were only placeholders and the errors render somewhere off screen.

The W3C states that WCAG applies to web content on mobile, and that meeting the standard means meeting testable success criteria. The criteria sit under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. [The WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the document to design toward. A phone pass can treat the operable part as concrete. The control can be reached. It has a visible name. Focus is not trapped inside a menu that will not close. That is a design bar for the redesign. It is not a certificate, and the review should not pretend it is one.

Sticky bars deserve a hard look. A strip that keeps a logo on screen by consuming a large share of a phone has taken the offer's place. If something stays fixed, it should be short, and it should usually be the action you are asking for.

## How a desktop-first team changes the week

Change the order of critique. The first review happens with a phone in someone's hand. The second review is the wide layout, checked to confirm it is the same page with more room. A critique that only gathers around a monitor will approve the wide picture and discover the phone later, when changing it is costly.

Describe breakpoints as behavior. At the narrow width, navigation collapses, cards stack, and the image sits below the headline. At the wide width, the image can sit beside the headline and the cards can form a row. If you cannot say the behavior in a sentence, the layout is still only a picture.

Set type sizes for the phone first. A display size chosen for a billboard hero often breaks a short offer into many lines, which slows the read the page is supposed to earn. Let the wide size grow from the size that already works in the hand.

Test with the real words. A headline that fits the wireframe and wraps badly in the true offer is a failed frame. Long product names, a two-line promise, and the actual button label are the content. Placeholder text hides the wrap until the week you can least afford to see it.

## The pass before you ship

Repeat the phone check on the staging site, on a device, on a ordinary connection. A smooth file on office wifi can still be a heavy page outside. Look at the first screen. Tap the action. Send one real submission to the inbox that will receive customers. Confirm the page does not jump when the photographs arrive.

The phone pass sits inside a larger review. When you want the brief, the primary action, and a stranger's reading in one meeting, use [how to review a redesign before it ships](/blog/review-a-redesign-before-launch).

When the redesign should be drawn from the phone outward and then built, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The narrow screen is the first composition, and the code should match it.
